```{r library setup}
#install.packages("ggplot2") # in case someone doesn't have it yet

library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2movies)
```

# Movie dataset initial exploration

This dataset is taken from the package `ggplot2movies`. [link to the
description
online](https://vincentarelbundock.github.io/Rdatasets/doc/ggplot2movies/movies.html)

The data contains: - 58,788 movies (rows) - 24 columns: - Movie title -
Year - Length (minutes) - Budget - Rating - Votes - r1-10 (percentile
per score 1-10, rounded to nearest 10%) - MPAA rating - Genre (action,
animation, comedy, drama, documentary, romance, short)

## The data

There are various ways to use the data from this package. We can load it
as `ggplot2movies::movies`, however, this does not store it as a
variable in our environment. So, we can assign it to a variable or we
can load it using `data` to store it as a variable

```{r, Load in data}

ggplot2movies::movies

# Store the data in the environment
movies <- ggplot2movies::movies

# This loads in the data from the package with the name "movies",
data("movies", package = "ggplot2movies")
# But sometimes takes a while
```

## Data exploration

The data contains:

- 58,788 movies (rows)

- 24 columns:

  - Movie title
  - Year
  - Length (minutes)
  - Budget
  - Rating
  - Votes
  - r1-10 (percentile per score 1-10, rounded to nearest 10%)
  - MPAA rating
  - Genre (action, animation, comedy, drama, documentary, romance,
    short)

```{r}
## Data initial exploration
head(movies)
dim(movies)
glimpse(movies)
class(movies)

# A cutoff of 50 removes 36075 movies 
cutoff_votes <- 50

# Change the datatype 
clean_movies <- movies |>   
  map(~str_trim(.x)) |>   
  as_tibble() |> 
  select(-budget, -mpaa) |> 
  mutate_at(vars(-title), as.numeric) |>  
  filter(votes >= cutoff_votes) 
  
class(clean_movies)
```

## Data manipulation

The variable "budget" contains many `NAs`, the variable "mpaa" also
contains a lot of empty characters. The genre variables appear to be
binary, but are loaded in as integers.

We have 7 rows indicating the genre of a movie, movies can have multiple
genres.

## Analysis plan

- We have a group of variables for the distribution of the rating.
- We have a group of variables for the genres.
- We have ratings and the number of votes.
- We have budget (but lots of NAs)
- We have movie lengths (in minutes)

It would be interesting to see the distribution of the ranks, in
relation to the number of voters. Then, we also have the information on
which year the movie was released.

**Ranks**

- How are the votes distributed (across the r1-10)?
- Can movie length predict scores + how many people watched it.

**Genre**

It would also be interesting to look at the popularity of the genres:

- Which movie genres has the highest overall scores?
- Which movie genre is voted on most (mean across the movies, min + max)
- How long are movies across genres (and does this influence the rank?)

**Decades**

Lastly, we can group per decade

- Which genres were popular along the decades?
- How many votes were there across the decades?
- Ratings across the decades? (overall, per genre)
- Did movie lengths change over the years?

These graphs can all be made interactive, with options for choosing
genres and decades, perhaps also with the possibility to select
double/triple genres (we will look into the distribution of multiple
genres), or to select certain years even (along with certain decades).

- Perhaps make it possible to select your own range of release years.

### Data manipulation

- We have 10 rows for the rating (r1 - r10)
- We have 7 rows indicating the genre of a movie, movies can have
  multiple genres.

Create subsets based on the movie genres

```{r}
movies_long <- pivot_longer(movies, cols = c(Action:Short), names_to = "genre", values_to = "genre_no_yes")
```

## Summary statistics

In the following table, basic statistics for the relevant numerical
variables in the dataset are summarised

```{r}

clean_movies %>% 
  select(2:5) %>% 
  pivot_longer(everything(), 
               names_to = "variable", 
               values_to ="value") %>%
  group_by(variable) %>% 
  summarise(
    Mean = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    Minimum = min(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    Maximum = max(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    Missing = sum(is.na(value))) 
  
```

## Visualize data distributions

The distribution of each relevant numerical variable can be visualized
in the following density graphs. These are: year, length, budget,
rating, and number of votes.

```{r}

density_distributions <- 
  clean_movies %>% 
  pivot_longer(
  cols = 2:5,   
  names_to = "variable",      
  values_to = "value"         
) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = value, fill = variable, colour = variable)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ variable, 
    scales = "free",
    strip.position = c("bottom"),
  labeller = as_labeller(c(
    "year" = "Year",
    "length"= "Length (min)",
    "rating"= "Rating",
    "votes"= "Number of votes"))) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + 
  theme(legend.position = "none", 
        strip.placement = "outside")

plot(density_distributions)
```

## Visualize rating patterns

We consider the 100 movies with the highest average rating and plot in a
heatmap the percentage of votes awarding 1-10 ratings. This will
visualize whether these top-rated movies have similar distribution
between rating points.

```{r}
library(superheat)

heatmap_rating <- 
  clean_movies %>% 
  select(title, rating, r1:r10) %>% 
  arrange(desc(rating)) %>% 
  slice_head(n = 100) %>% 
  {
    matrix_rating <- as.matrix(select(., r1:r10))
    rownames(matrix_rating) <- .$title
    superheat(
      matrix_rating,
      pretty.order.rows = FALSE,        
      yr = .$rating,                  
      yr.plot.type = "bar",
      yr.axis.name = "Average Rating",
      yr.bar.col = "lightblue4",
      heat.col.scheme = "viridis",
      grid.hline.col = "white",
      grid.vline.col = "white",
      left.label.text.size = 2.5,
      bottom.label.text.angle = 0
    )
  }
```

## Regression

### Impact of votes on rating

We want to investigate whether the total number of votes can predict the
average rating of a movie. We do this by fitting a linear model to the
data using votes as a predictor of rating.

```{r}
fit_votes <- 
  lm(rating ~ 1 + votes, 
     data = clean_movies) 

summary(fit_votes)

# Visualise diagnostic plots of the linear model in one figure. These assess the criteria of: linearity, homoscedasticity, normality, and absence of outliers
plot_lm_votes <- fit_votes %>% 
  {par(mfrow = c(2, 2));
    plot(.)}
```

Although the slope shows a low p-value, the adjusted R^2^ is low
(0.03139). The diagnostic plots indicate that the data may be not
linearly distributed or homoscedatic. We can try to fit a better model
using a log transformation.

```{r}
fit_votes_log <- 
  lm(rating ~ 1 + log(votes), 
     data = clean_movies) 

summary(fit_votes_log)

# Compare the adjusted R^2 of both models
summary(fit_votes_log)$adj.r.squared - 
  summary(fit_votes)$adj.r.squared   #log-transformed is higher

# Calculate Akaike's ‘An Information Criterion’ for both models
AIC(fit_votes, fit_votes_log) 
```

When we log-transform the votes variable, we obtain a slightly higher
adjusted R^2^ (0.04227) and the model is better according to the AIC
metric. Even if it remains weak, the correlation between amount of votes
and rating is better explained by this second model.

We can visualize the two predicted fit lines on the data in a scatter
plot of average rating against number of votes. Here, the votes are
colored by the percentage of users who awarded a 10/10 rate.

```{r}

votes_rating_plot <- ggplot(
  clean_movies, 
      aes(votes, rating)) +
      geom_point(aes(color = r10)) +
  labs(dictionary = c(
    votes = "Total user votes",
    rating = "Average rating /10",
    r10 = "Percentage of 10/10 votes")) +
  stat_smooth(method = "lm", 
              formula = y ~ 1 + x, 
              se = FALSE, 
              color = "orange3", 
              linetype = 1) +
  stat_smooth(method = "lm", 
              formula = y ~ 1 + log(x), 
              se = FALSE, 
              color = "red3", 
              linetype = 1) + 
  scale_color_viridis_c()

print(votes_rating_plot)
```

#### Impact of 10/10 votes on average rating

We also investigate whether the percentage of users who awarded a 10/10
rating (r10 variable) can predict the average rating of a movie.

```{r}
fit_r10 <- 
  lm(rating ~ 1 + r10, 
     data = clean_movies) 

summary(fit_r10)

# Visualise diagnostic plots of the linear model in one figure
plot_lm_r10 <- fit_r10 %>% 
  {par(mfrow = c(2, 2));
    plot(.)}
# no clear violations of the requirements
```

The low p-value and adjusted R^2^ of 0.1789 reveal a correlation,
although weak, between r10 and rating. This can be visualized on the
following scatter plot of the r10 data.

```{r}
r10_rating_plot <- ggplot(
  clean_movies, 
      aes(r10, rating)) +
      geom_point() +
  labs(dictionary = c(
    rating = "Average rating /10",
    r10 = "Percentage of 10/10 votes")) +
  stat_smooth(method = "lm", 
              formula = y ~ 1 + x, 
              se = FALSE, 
              color = "red3", 
              linetype = 1)

print(r10_rating_plot)
```
